busy_loop.title: {name} keeps Home Assistant busy
busy_loop.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, {name} used the event loop for {ms} ms a minute, {share}% of all CPU time on the event loop. While it runs, everything else waits: automations, the dashboard and other integrations.

What you can do:
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.
- If {name} is set up on the integrations page, [disable it]({config_url}) for a while and compare.

loop_blocked.title: Home Assistant stood still for {ms} ms in {name}
loop_blocked.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, the event loop stood still for {ms} ms at a stretch. The code running at that moment belonged to {name}, in {function}. While the loop stands still, nothing else in Home Assistant moves: no automation, no dashboard update, no other integration. A stop this long is usually a call that waits on the network or a file without yielding.

What you can do:
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.
- If {name} is set up on the integrations page, [disable it]({config_url}) for a while and compare.

busy_states.title: {name} changes state too often
busy_states.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, {name} changed the state of its entities {per_min} times a minute, {attributes_only} of them only in their attributes. Each change reaches the recorder, which stores a new row, the dashboard and every automation that watches the entity. Devices rarely change that often. This usually means the integration passes on every reading, including attributes such as timestamps or signal strength. Writes that change nothing are cheap and not counted here.

What you can do:
- Check the options of {name} for an update interval.
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.

Each change reaches the recorder, which stores a new row, the dashboard and every automation that watches the entity. Devices rarely change that often. This usually means the integration passes on every reading, including attributes such as timestamps or signal strength. Writes that change nothing are cheap and not counted here.

What you can do:
- If {name} polls, polling can be turned off in its system options. Its entities then update only when an automation asks for it.
- {name} is part of Home Assistant and updates with it. Check whether a newer Home Assistant fixes it.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the Home Assistant issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.

loop_waits.title: The event loop often waits
loop_waits.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, the event loop was busy {ms} ms a minute longer than it used the CPU. It was waiting: on a blocking call such as reading a file or the network, on a busy thread that held Python's interpreter lock, or for a free CPU core. Home Assistant does nothing else while it waits.

What you can do:
- Look in the log for "Detected blocking call", which names the integration.
- In the CPU view, open the integrations at the top. Wall time under "Event loop callbacks" far above their "Loop ms/min" points to the one that waits.

growing_resources.title: {name} may be leaking
growing_resources.description:
Between the last two memory snapshots {name} added {what} and did not release them. If this keeps growing over hours, memory use rises until Home Assistant restarts.

What you can do:
- Take another snapshot later.
- If the numbers keep growing, report it at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}) with the report from this page.
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.

big_attributes.title: {name} writes large attributes
big_attributes.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, the entities of {name} changed attributes worth {kib} KiB a minute, counted each time they change and as the recorder serializes them. Open dashboards receive the attributes that changed. The recorder does not store attributes over 16 KiB and logs a warning for every such change instead.

What you can do:
- Exclude the entities from the recorder if you do not need their history.
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.

noisy_logs.title: {name} logs many warnings
noisy_logs.description:
Over the last {minutes} minutes, {per_min} warnings and errors a minute were logged by or about {name}, {errors} of them errors. Each one is formatted and written to the log, and a steady stream hides the messages that matter.

What you can do:
- Open the log and look at what it reports. Often it is a device that cannot be reached or a setting that needs attention.
- Check whether an update of {name} is available.
- Look for a report, or open one, at [the issue tracker]({issues_url}), and add the report from this page.
